title: What Is Next For Micron Stock?

What Is Next For Micron Stock?

Shares of Micron Technology (MU) have returned 415% over the past twelve months, easily outpacing the 17.3% return for the S&P 500. Yet the stock trades at just 13.2 times earnings, well below the 21.9 multiple of the broader index. Buyers appear unsure that profits made during a memory shortage will last, and the company has been working on exactly that problem. So what is Micron doing to make those profits last?

Micron Has Long-Term Agreements For Its Memory

Micron has secured long-term agreements covering both DRAM and NAND memory chips through 2030. Executives used their September 30 call to discuss extending these commitments beyond 2030.

A question during that September 30 call indicated the company holds 26 of these agreements, including ten signed in fiscal Q4 2026.

These contracts depart from standard orders by altering how the memory is priced. Management noted that about three quarters of the revenue under these deals relies on a defined pricing framework, with most of those frameworks setting a floor and a ceiling.

Agreements Could Cover A Third Of 2030 Sales

A question during the fiscal Q4 2026 call described the agreements as covering 35% of Micron's sales by 2030. Management did not dispute the figure, saying the DRAM share is a little under 35% and the NAND share a little above it. Reaching that threshold would mark a structural shift for a business whose results have historically swung widely.

The company posted an operating margin of 74.6% over the past twelve months, yet three years ago its operations ran at a loss of 35% of sales. Top-line results have fluctuated just as violently, with fiscal Q4 2026 revenue climbing 379.3% from a year earlier.

Applying a price floor to a subset of sales would not eliminate swings like those, but it could limit them. The agreements also fall short of an absolute guarantee, as about a quarter of their revenue remains open to periodic negotiation or moves with market prices.

The stock does not appear to reflect steadier profits yet. Despite the twelve-month gain, Micron shares sit 18.5% below their 52-week high. They returned 0.6% over the past three months, trailing the 3.8% return for the S&P 500.

First Idaho Output Is Due In Mid-2027

Micron expects its Idaho facility to yield its first output in mid-2027, while a new clean room is scheduled to come online in the second half of 2028. More supply is exactly what worries investors. Barron's wrote on October 6 that Micron stock is cheap because investors are wary of what happens when memory-chip production increases.

title: How Much Of Qualcomm Stock Rides On One Business?
detail:
How Much Of Qualcomm Stock Rides On One Business?

QCOM
AAPL
AVGO
NVDA
INTC
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Image from Pixabay

Phone chip revenue is the central metric to watch at Qualcomm (QCOM). Handset chips generated $5.1 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, accounting for more than half of the company's $9.9 billion in revenue. Total revenue fell 4.0% from a year earlier, and a segment that makes up more than half of sales deserves close attention. So what is hurting Qualcomm's phone chip sales?

Qualcomm Faces Costlier Memory And Less Apple Business

Qualcomm management detailed two causes on its fiscal Q3 2026 call. The memory chip market presents the first hurdle. Management said memory conditions across the global smartphone market affected handset revenue. CNBC reported on September 22, 2026 that the smartphone industry is contracting because of skyrocketing memory prices. Alongside these broader conditions, management said revenue from Android phone chips dropped 20% from a year earlier.

The second issue centers on Apple. Qualcomm said on its July earnings call that it expected its share of the upcoming iPhone launch to be materially lower than its earlier estimate of 20%. The company also expected Apple revenue to drop faster starting in fiscal Q4 2026.

This slowdown is already visible in Qualcomm's total revenue. After growing 10.0% and then 5.0% in the first two of the last four quarters, revenue fell 3.5% and then 4.0% in the final two periods.

Reduced business from Apple also alters the seasonal shape of Qualcomm's year. The fiscal first quarter was traditionally the strongest period. Management told investors not to expect that pattern now, as Apple's strong December quarter is missing from the current forecast.

Can Qualcomm Make Up For Weaker Phone Chips?

Management asserts it can bridge the gap, yet the answer relies heavily on forecasts. The company has reported growth outside of phones thus far. Chip sales outside handsets, which include automotive and connected devices, grew 28% from a year earlier in fiscal Q3 2026. Automotive revenue alone hit $1.6 billion, up 61%. Within the phone segment itself, management estimates that chip sales to Chinese phone makers reached a bottom in fiscal Q3.

Qualcomm has not yet proven that this growth can replace Apple. Management expects growth outside handsets in fiscal 2027 to replace the Apple revenue of fiscal 2026. That fiscal 2027 forecast includes data center revenue growing to $5 billion in a market Qualcomm is entering now. Management acknowledged that investors want more proof it can deliver there as a new entrant.

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) closed at $101.35 on Monday after a 3.20% session decline. It reached an intraday low of $100.71 and slipped to $100.18 after hours, just above the round number chart watchers have been tracking.

Shutterstock

The stock now sits 20.4% below its September 24 close of $127.39, which was its highest since early August. It is also 28% below its record close of $140.94, set on June 22.

Those are large drops for a company worth $532.55 billion. Even so, Intel is still up 178.66% over the past year, so this drawdown sits inside a large rally.

The stock has fallen in six of the last seven sessions. The selling likely reflects a market repricing a story that ran ahead of the evidence before earnings.

INTC Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
Four Headlines Knocked Intel Off Its September Peak

On October 4, Elon Musk confirmed talks about Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) joining his Terafab chip project, which Intel had joined in April. Musk said: "Just discussions, but something may come of it."

Intel said it "would continue to participate in Terafab," but the stock fell more than 4% the next session. Intel's foundry dream depends on being the chosen alternative manufacturer, and a second alternative inside the same project reduces that role.
